replies: Saved: Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau and did 2 years of reporting. Is that right?

Your skills match several core needs for a data analyst role.

Matches (strong)
- SQL — essential for querying databases and building datasets.
- Excel — required for data cleaning, quick analysis, pivot tables and ad-hoc reporting.
- Tableau — fits visualization and dashboarding responsibilities.

Matches (experience)
- 2 years of reporting — directly relevant: shows practical experience producing reports, tracking metrics and delivering insights on a schedule.
Common additional skills employers expect (gaps to address)
- Data cleaning/ETL tools or processes (e.g., Python/pandas, R, Airflow) — many roles want hands-on cleaning or pipeline work.
- Statistical analysis and A/B testing — helpful for deeper insights and experimentation roles.
- SQL beyond basics (performance, window functions, CTEs) — many jobs expect intermediate/advanced SQL.
- Business/domain knowledge and stakeholder communication — being able to translate data into action for nontechnical teams.
- Version control, reproducible analyses, unit testing of analyses — less common but a plus.
- Cloud/warehouse experience (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) — increasingly requested.
One next step: tell me which of those gaps you already have (e.g., Python, advanced SQL, BigQuery, statistics) or paste a short resume and I’ll mark the exact strengths to highlight and the 2–3 things to add before you apply.

You don't have any Lincoln International interviews or tasks on file yet. The one step that starts a tracked prep is: paste the interview invite or tell me the date/time and who you'll meet so I can record it and make a targeted plan.

Prep now — quick mock and targeted notes:

1) Tell me the panel format (or pick a default): behavioral + technical case (default I'll assume 1 partner + 1 associate, 45–60 min, mix of fit and a 15–20 min modeling/case). Is that right? (yes/no)

Meanwhile, here's the prep I’ll run with that default (do these now; last item is a 5-question mock you can answer in this chat):
A. 6-point brief you must have ready (say these aloud; short bullets)
- Why Lincoln International, now: one sentence tying their deal focus/size/sector to your background and career aim. (One-liner example I can write if you tell me your background.)
- Why you: 2 strengths with an example each (analytical rigor, client communication, transaction support). Use CAR: Context, Action you took, Result (metric if possible).
- Top deal you worked on: 60–90 second story with your role, the key analytical or client challenge, what you did, and the outcome.
- Technical fundamentals: valuation (DCF steps and key drivers), accretion/dilution basics, LBO mechanics (equity check, IRR drivers) — one sentence each.
- Excel/modeling confidence: what you can build under time pressure (three things: e.g., build an LBO with sources & uses, quick sensitivity table, cleanly link P&L to cashflow).
- Questions for interviewers: two that show commercial curiosity and fit (one about deal team structure / exit strategies, one about how Lincoln differentiates on mid-market mandates).
B. Technical cheat-sheet to memorize (one-line definitions)
- DCF: forecast unlevered FCF -> WACC discount -> terminal value (exit multiple or Gordon growth) -> enterprise value -> subtract debt + add cash = equity value.
- WACC drivers: cost of equity (beta, market premium), cost of debt (post-tax), capital structure weights.
- LBO key levers: purchase price, debt level & terms, operational improvements, exit multiple; IRR increases with higher leverage, higher exit multiple, and shorter hold.
- Accretion/dilution: compare pro-forma EPS to acquirer EPS; accretive if pro-forma EPS > acquirer EPS (watch for purchase accounting, financing assumptions).
- Comparable comps: pick the right peer set (size, growth, margins) and explain outliers.

C. 3 common behavioral questions + model answers (structure I’ll score)
- "Tell me about yourself." — 45–60s: quick arc (education → relevant experience → recent role accomplishments → why this role).
- "Tell me about a time you had conflicting priorities." — single example, what you chose, trade-offs, outcome and what you learned.
- "Tell me about a time you made a mistake on a deal." — take ownership, fix steps, concrete mitigation, what you changed.
D. Case/calc checks interviewers love (practice)
- Walk me through a simple DCF aloud: I’ll stop you on missing pieces.
- Quick Fermi estimates: e.g., estimate market size for a niche manufacturing business (show assumptions).
- Mini modeling task: given revenue, margin, capex %, build a 3-year cash flow sketch and say how valuation moves with growth vs margin.

E. 5-question mock (I'll score each answer: structure, evidence, specificity). First question here now:
"Walk me through your resume in 60 seconds, focusing on the skills that make you a strong analyst at Lincoln International." Answer now and I’ll score and give one fix, then ask the next.
One question: confirm interview format — is the default (1 partner + 1 associate, 45–60 min, fit + technical/case) right, or tell me the real format from your invite?

You don't have any applications or a queued posting on file yet. The one step that starts one is: paste the job posting link (or tell me its exact title and company) you mean by "the first one."

When you name that specific posting I'll read it and then prepare the application card. Here is exactly, field by field, what I will fill or show on that card and how I decide each item (I assumed a standard online employer form — say if the posting uses email instead):
1) Employer / Job title — copied exactly from the posting (I will not change this).
2) Job location / on-site-remote status — copied from the posting (if multiple locations, I list each).
3) Resume file — I will show which saved resume file you want to use; if you haven't supplied one I leave this blank and ask you to paste or pick one. I will not attach anything you didn't confirm.
4) Cover letter / short note to employer — I will draft a 1–3 paragraph cover note (and a ≤120-word email version if the application is by email). Wherever I lack a fact I use [brackets] (for example, [two-sentence reason I want this role]). You approve or edit it on the card.
5) Name, Email, Phone — I will fill these exactly from the contact you saved for your resumes. If you haven't saved contact info, the card leaves them blank for you to type. I will not guess or pull your account email.
6) LinkedIn profile URL — filled only if you previously saved it as a confirmed field; otherwise blank.
7) Work authorization / visa status — left blank unless you confirm it now; the card will mark it required if the employer asks. I will not invent statuses.
8) Minimum salary / salary expectation (if asked) — left blank unless you give a number now; I never invent pay. I can suggest market-range wording, but you must pick or type it on the card.
9) Earliest start date — left blank unless you give it; I will offer typical formats (e.g., "Available immediately" or "Two weeks' notice").
10) Screening questions (yes/no, multiple choice, short text) — I will prefill suggested answers where your confirmed facts let me; otherwise they remain for you to complete on the card. Each suggested answer is marked as "please check."
11) Attachments (portfolio, certificates, transcripts) — I will list attachments you confirmed to include and leave the attach slots empty if you haven't provided them. Portfolio links are pasted into the portfolio field; files must be provided by you.
12) Additional optional message to recruiter — I will draft a 1–2 sentence optional message (e.g., "Happy to discuss how my [skill] at [employer] maps to this role") with [brackets] for missing specifics. You must approve.
13) Resume parsing / profile fields (if the form extracts fields from your resume) — I will show exactly which parsed fields the form would fill (title, company, dates) and highlight anything that conflicts with your confirmed facts so you can correct it before submit.
14) Diversity / self-ID questions and consent checkboxes — shown exactly as the employer requires; I will not fill them for you.
15) Privacy/data-consent and opt-in checkboxes — shown exactly; the card will ask you to confirm before submitting.
16) CAPTCHA / security steps — the card will note these if the employer requires them; you complete them on the employer page when approving. I won't bypass them.
17) Submit method note — a plain line that says how the application will be sent (via the employer form, by upload to an ATS, or by email to a recruiter). If email is required but your email connection isn't enabled, the card will say sending by email is blocked until you connect your email.
18) What will be saved to your account — I list every item that will be stored (the resume used, the cover note text, attachments, answers to screening questions) and where (application record).
19) What will NOT be sent unless you approve — a clear line: nothing is sent until you click approve in your browser extension.
20) Any required edits or missing facts — a short checklist (e.g., "Add work authorization", "Choose resume file", "Confirm phone number") you must complete before the card allows sending.
What I assume for this draft: a standard employer online application form with typical fields. If the posting instead is an email address to send materials to, I'll prepare an email version (subject line, ≤120-word body, attachments listed) instead — say which you prefer.

Next step: paste the job posting link or tell me the exact title and company for the "first one," and paste or point to the resume you want attached. One question: which posting is the first one?
